title: Oil Breaches $100 as Red Sea Attacks Reignite Supply Fears
summary: Global oil prices surged past $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May, driven by Houthi militia attacks on oil tankers in the Red Sea. The strikes jeopardize a critical Saudi export corridor that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz, reigniting fears of supply disruptions amid the widening Middle East conflict. The benchmark UK gas price has also climbed sharply, reaching around 150 pence per therm—up from 98p at the end of June. The rally reverses a brief dip that followed a now-collapsed U.S.-Iran ceasefire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week that Iranian leaders are "not ready to make a deal," dimming hopes for de-escalation. For consumers, the impact is immediate: U.S. average gasoline prices have topped $4 a gallon again, according to AAA, and analysts warn of broader ripple effects. "More expensive fuel and energy can ripple through the wider economy, increasing costs for businesses and ultimately feeding through into the price of food and other goods," said Jonathan Raymond of Quilter Cheviot. This creates a dilemma for central banks. Kevin Warsh, the newly appointed Federal Reserve chair, told Congress the Fed has "no tolerance to persistently elevated inflation," signaling that interest rates—currently at 3.5%-3.75%—may stay higher for longer. In the UK, economists expect the Bank of England to hold rates steady, though cuts could come next year if energy prices ease. The situation underscores how geopolitical turmoil can swiftly translate into household financial strain, from pricier fill-ups to costlier groceries, leaving policymakers with few good options.
why_it_matters: Oil price shocks affect not just drivers but the entire economy, potentially raising the cost of food, travel, and borrowing, which hits families directly. Understanding these connections shows why wars far away can quickly become a problem at home.

background_read: The Red Sea is a critical route for oil tankers traveling from the Persian Gulf to Europe and North America via the Suez Canal; attacks there can disrupt global energy supplies.

The Houthi militia in Yemen, which is supported by Iran, began targeting commercial ships in late 2023 in response to the Israel-Hamas war, causing many vessels to reroute around southern Africa at much higher cost.
The Strait of Hormuz, which the Red Sea route bypasses, is a narrow channel controlled by Iran and Oman; any conflict there has historically threatened oil markets.
Kevin Warsh, whom President Trump appointed as Federal Reserve chair in 2025, must now balance the risk of rising energy-driven inflation against a slowing economy.
In the UK, the benchmark gas price measured in pence per therm can affect home heating bills; similar spikes occurred during the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022.

perspectives.description: Some oil-producing countries and companies benefit from high prices, earning more revenue. Investors in energy stocks also gain, and governments that rely on oil exports can use the windfall to fund public spending.

Higher gasoline and heating costs strain household budgets, especially for lower-income families. The ripple effects push up food, transportation, and goods prices, making everyday life more expensive and potentially leading to public discontent.

Oil prices are historically volatile and often reflect geopolitical risk. This time, the Red Sea attacks represent a persistent threat rather than a one-time shock, so markets may build a lasting ‘fear premium’ that keeps prices elevated even without actual supply shortages.

If Houthi attacks continue, the world might accelerate the shift to renewable energy to reduce dependence on unstable regions, but in the short term, governments may release strategic oil reserves to cool prices. Central banks face a tough choice: contain inflation or support growth, and their decisions will shape economic prospects for years ahead.
